title: Gravadlax
subtitle: Scandinavian salt and dill cured fish
excerpt: A whole fish fillet is packed in a dry cure of salt, sugar, dill, and crushed peppercorns and left for 48 hours until silky and translucent. Gravadlax means 'buried salmon' in Old Norse. The result is extraordinary for such simple preparation.
sourceNotes: Gravadlax means 'buried salmon' in Old Norse. Medieval fishermen preserved fish by burying it in salt underground. The modern version uses a dry cure of salt, sugar, and dill. A Scandinavian staple for centuries.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 48 hours ahead. Will keep in the fridge for 5 days once cured.

content.text: Gravadlax is mostly waiting. The actual work takes 20 minutes -- the curing does the rest. Wrap tightly and weigh the fish down with tins or heavy pots so the cure presses in evenly. Slice very thinly on an angle to serve.

items.prepNote: use a 500g salmon fillet if available -- this recipe is designed for salmon

content.text: Mix salt flakes, caster sugar, lemon zest, and crushed peppercorns together in a small bowl.
Lay the fish fillet skin-side down on a large sheet of cling film. Spread the chopped dill evenly over the flesh. Pack the salt cure mixture on top of the dill.
Wrap very tightly in the cling film, then wrap again in a second layer. Place on a tray and weigh down with another tray stacked with tins or heavy pots.
Refrigerate for 48 hours, turning the parcel over halfway through.
Unwrap. Scrape off the dill and cure. Pat dry with kitchen paper. Slice very thinly at a low angle. Serve with mustard, soured cream, and rye bread.

items.cause: Cure left on too long or too much salt used
items.fix: Rinse the cured fish briefly under cold water and pat dry before slicing.

content.text: Scandinavia. A classic starter across Sweden, Denmark, and Norway. The Swedish version uses more dill than Norwegian or Danish. Served at midsummer celebrations and on open sandwiches at every Swedish smorgasbord.
